column41: No, BUT! Did you know that there is a chance we could lose the ability to produce any drug/medicine we depend on??? For example, Ritonavir "disappeared" in 1998 because a new, more stable crystal form (Form II) unexpectedly emerged, contaminating production facilities and making the original, soluble form (Form I) impossible to produce. This phenomenon, known as a "disappearing polymorph," meant the drug's crystals became too insoluble for the body to absorb. The new, more stable Form II crystal likely formed and contaminated manufacturing equipment. Once Form II existed, it acted as a "seed" (even in tiny amounts) that turned all subsequent production into the unwanted form. If you wanna learn more about this, you can watch this video (https://youtu.be/ksn5yrsC3Wg?si=74aW8yB6dmX614_z) by Veritasium called “The disaster I never imaged having to worry about”.

column41: Nah, but did ya know!!! While cannibalism is almost universally taboo today, evidence of the practice dating back over 600,000 years! The Fore people of Papua New Guinea practiced "endocannibalism" (consuming deceased relatives as a sign of respect and to cleanse their spirits) until the late 1950s. This custom led to an outbreak of kuru, a devastating, incurable prion disease similar to mad cow disease, which was spread by eating the infected brain tissue of deceased family members. However, over centuries, some Fore people developed a genetic mutation that grants them complete immunity to these prions. Cannibalism wasn't always a savage practice; it was highly institutionalized in early modern Europe. During the 17th century and up to the 19th century, Europeans consumed human body parts, blood, and even "skull moss" (moss that grew on the skulls of hanged men) as medicine to treat conditions like nosebleeds, epilepsy, and headaches. Yummy… From a purely biological perspective, human flesh isn't particularly nutritious compared to other megafauna. Who would have guessed 🤷‍♀️ some studies estimates that an average adult human body contains roughly 126,000 calories! Early human ancestors or prehistoric tribes likely relied on human flesh for ritualistic, symbolic, or territorial reasons rather than as a primary source of caloric intake. Interestingly, there are no federal laws in the United States that explicitly outlaw cannibalism per se. Instead, consuming another human is heavily prohibited because of the laws that make it a crime to obtain human flesh legally (such as charges for desecration of a corpse, murder, or illegal transport of body parts! Did you know Did you know? The village of Grand Coulee, Saskatchewan, sees an estimated 6–12 freight trains pass through every day, adding up to roughly 2,000–4,000 trains each year.

The most common trains you’ll see are grain trains  the iconic prairie trains that can stretch 100+ cars long as they haul Saskatchewan’s agricultural products across the country. A single grain train can carry the equivalent of thousands of truckloads of grain, making rail an essential part of moving prairie crops to market.

The railway is also a big reason Grand Coulee exists today. Like many Saskatchewan communities, it grew around the rail line, which connected local farmers, businesses, and residents to the rest of the province and beyond.

The flat terrain is one of the reasons the area became such productive farmland — and it also created the perfect setting for the railway to run straight across the prairie.

Did you know Lightning is hotter than the surface of the Sun?

When lightning strikes, the air around the bolt can heat up to around 30,000 K (53,500°F)—that’s roughly 5 times hotter than the surface of the Sun, which is about 5,500°C (10,000°F)! 

That extreme heat causes the air to expand explosively, creating the shockwave we hear as thunder. So every time you hear thunder, you’re actually hearing the atmosphere rapidly reacting to a burst of energy that is hotter than the Sun’s surface. 

While lightning is much hotter than the surface of the Sun, it is nowhere near as hot as the Sun's core, which reaches about 15 million degrees Celsius. Unlike the  Sun that stays hot all the time because of constant nuclear fusion. Lightning is only hot for a tiny fraction of a second

Did you know that Saturn is so light for its enormous size that, if you had a bathtub big enough to hold the entire planet, Saturn would actually float in water?! 
Saturn is the second-largest planet in our solar system and is about nine times wider than Earth, but its average density is only about 0.69 grams per cubic centimetre, compared with water’s 1 gram per cubic centimetre. That means Saturn is, on average, less dense than water. The reason is that Saturn is a gas giant, made mostly of hydrogen and helium, rather than solid rock like Earth. Its enormous amount of material is spread out over an absolutely gigantic volume, making it surprisingly “fluffy” for such a massive planet. Of course, you’d need a bathtub so ridiculously enormous that the plumbing industry would probably quit on the spot and Saturn’s gravity would make the whole experiment completely impossible but as a physics thought experiment, Saturn would float

Did you know Mercury Has a Magnetic Field? 

Even though Mercury is a small, rocky planet, it has its own magnetic field something scientists didn’t expect from such a tiny world! Mercury has an enormous iron-rich core, and part of that core is still liquid. As the molten metal moves around deep inside the planet, it creates a magnetic field, similar to how Earth’s magnetic field is generated. Mercury’s magnetic field is much weaker than Earth’s, but it’s strong enough to interact with the solar wind from the Sun.

Basically, Mercury is a tiny planet with a surprisingly active, molten heart!
